b2018-1.ask: 3 arrows fly straight across, popping every balloon they touch. How many balloons are never hit?
steps: Follow each arrow's line all the way across the picture with your finger.
Every balloon on that line gets popped (the arrow keeps going).
Mark the popped balloons on all three lines.
Count the balloons that no line touches: 3.
b2018-1.spot: Lines across a picture? Extend each line and see what it touches.
b2018-1.oops: Thinking an arrow stops after one balloon.

b2018-2.ask: What does Peter see when he looks down on the table from above?
steps: From above, you see only the tops of things.
The long block looks like a long rectangle.
The round can looks like a circle, and the box looks like a square.
Check where each one sits: circle on one side in front, square at the other end at the back. That's C.
b2018-2.check: Compare the positions in C with the 3D picture. Each object is in the right spot. ✓
b2018-2.spot: Views from above? Each object turns into its top shape.
b2018-2.oops: Mixing up which end the circle and square are on.

b2018-3.ask: Two arrows in the middle ring scored 14. A middle-ring arrow and a centre arrow scored 16. Two centre arrows score how much?
steps: Two middle-ring hits = 14, so one middle-ring hit = 7.
Centre + middle = 16, so the centre = 16 − 7 = 9.
Two centre hits: 9 + 9 = 18.
b2018-3.spot: Two scores sharing a part? Find the part you can, then swap it in.

b2018-4.ask: Two snails start at corner S going opposite ways around the garden, one at 1 m/h, one at 2 m/h. Where do they meet?
steps: Count the perimeter of the garden on the grid: 24 m.
Together they cover 1 + 2 = 3 m every hour.
They meet when together they've gone all the way around: 24 ÷ 3 = 8 hours.
The slow snail went 8 m: up 2, then 6 along the top. That's point B.
b2018-4.check: The fast snail went 16 m the other way and also lands on B. ✓
b2018-4.spot: Two things moving toward each other? Add their speeds.
b2018-4.oops: Forgetting they go in opposite directions.

b2018-5.ask: ▢3 − 2▢ = 25 with two hidden digits. What do the hidden digits add to?
steps: Turn it into adding: ▢3 = 25 + 2▢.
Ones column: 5 + ▢ ends in 3. 5 + 8 = 13, so the hidden digit is 8.
25 + 28 = 53, so the first hidden digit is 5.
b2018-5.spot: Hidden digits in a subtraction? Flip it into an addition.
b2018-5.oops: Forgetting the carry into the tens.

b2018-6.ask: A star is a square with 4 equal-sided triangles on its sides. The square's perimeter is 36 cm. What's the star's perimeter?
steps: Square side: 36 ÷ 4 = 9 cm.
Each triangle has all sides equal, so each side is also 9 cm.
Each triangle shows 2 sides on the outside of the star. 4 triangles × 2 = 8 sides.
b2018-6.check: The star's outline is exactly twice the square's: 2 × 36 = 72. ✓
b2018-6.spot: Shapes stuck together? Count only the edges on the outside.
b2018-6.oops: Counting the square's sides too. They're hidden inside.

b2018-7.ask: An ink spot covers a calendar. You can see the 3rd is a Friday. What day is the 25th?
steps: The same weekday comes every 7 days.
The 25th is the day after Friday: Saturday.
b2018-7.oops: Counting day by day and slipping.

b2018-8.ask: How many times must you roll a die to be SURE a result repeats?
steps: Be unlucky Ulysses: roll as many different numbers as possible.
A die has 6 numbers. You could roll 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6: six rolls, no repeat.
The 7th roll must match one of them.
b2018-8.check: 6 rolls can all be different; 7 can't. ✓
b2018-8.spot: 'To be sure'? Imagine the unluckiest results, then add one.
b2018-8.oops: Saying 6. Six rolls could all be different.

b2018-9.ask: Three squares fit together. The smallest has side 6 cm. How long is the biggest square's side?
steps: Write every length you know on the picture. The smallest square's side is 6 cm.
The square next to it is 2 cm shorter where they line up, so one piece of the big square's side is 6 − 2 = 4 cm.
The other piece is 2 cm plus another 6 cm side: 2 + 6 = 8 cm.
The big square's side is 4 + 8 = 12 cm, twice the small square.
b2018-9.spot: Squares fitting together? Label every side and use the edges that line up.
b2018-9.oops: Guessing from how big it looks.

b2018-10.ask: Touching a light bulb lights it and all its neighbours. Fewest touches to light every bulb?
steps: Count each bulb's neighbours: every bulb has only 2 or 3.
So touching one bulb lights at most 4 of the 8 bulbs. 1 touch can't do it.
Touch a bulb with 3 neighbours: 4 bulbs light up.
Pick a second bulb on the other side whose neighbours are the 4 still dark. 2 touches light all 8.
b2018-10.check: Point at each bulb: it's one of the two you touched, or a neighbour of one. ✓
b2018-10.spot: Covering everything? Start with the most connected piece.
b2018-10.oops: Touching bulbs one at a time without planning.

b2018-11.ask: In which square is the black-to-white ratio the biggest?
steps: Each big square is cut into the same small triangles. Count black and white pieces in each.
Square A: black is 1/4 of the square. White is 3/4.
Check B, C and D: the black triangles add up to 1/4 of the square in each one too.
So every square is 1 black to 3 white.
b2018-11.check: Move the black triangles in your head: in each square they fill exactly one corner quarter. ✓
b2018-11.spot: Comparing areas? Count in equal small pieces.
b2018-11.oops: Thinking the squares with more black triangles have more black. The triangles are smaller.

b2018-12.ask: Nine cars drive off following their arrows. Which picture shows them afterwards?
steps: Look at each car's arrow: straight, left or right.
Count how many cars end up on each road after turning.
Check each answer picture: does each road have the right number of cars?
Only picture B matches.
b2018-12.check: Count cars on every road in B and compare with your list. ✓
b2018-12.spot: Lots of things moving? Count where they end up, road by road.
b2018-12.oops: Turning cars the wrong way. Imagine you're the driver.

b2018-13.ask: Four of 1 to 5 fill spots so both arrow calculations give 8. Which number is under the star?
steps: The top path: green + pink − blue = 8. The bottom path: green × red ÷ blue = 8.
Try blue = 1 (simplest): green × red = 8, so green and red are 2 and 4.
Top: green + pink = 9. If green = 4, pink = 5. If green = 2, pink = 7 (not allowed).
So pink (the star) = 5.
b2018-13.spot: Missing numbers in a calculation? Try small numbers in the trickiest spot first.
b2018-13.oops: Forgetting each number can be used only once.

b2018-14.ask: A lion is behind one of 3 doors. Only one sign is true. Door 1: 'Not here.' Door 2: 'Here.' Door 3: 'Two and three is five.' Where's the lion?
steps: Door 3's sign is ALWAYS true: 2 + 3 = 5.
Only one sign is true, so door 1's and door 2's signs are false.
Door 1 false: the lion IS behind door 1.
Door 2 false: the lion is not behind door 2. That fits.
b2018-14.check: Lion behind door 1: sign 1 false, sign 2 false, sign 3 true. Exactly one true. ✓
b2018-14.spot: True and false signs? Find a sign that's definitely true (or false) first.
b2018-14.oops: Ignoring door 3 because it isn't about the lion.

b2018-16.ask: Any two cells sharing an edge in the triangle table add to the same number. Two cells are filled (2 and 3). What's the total?
steps: If neighbours always add to the same number, then all the pointing-up triangles hold the same number, and all the pointing-down triangles hold the same number.
So one kind is 2 and the other kind is 3.
Count: there are 6 pointing-up triangles and 3 pointing-down triangles. The 2 is in an up-triangle and the 3 in a down-triangle.
b2018-16.spot: 'Neighbours always add the same'? Neighbours of neighbours are equal.
b2018-16.oops: Thinking you need more numbers to work it out.

b2018-17.ask: Monday, Alexandra sends a picture to 5 friends. Each day everyone who just got it sends it to 2 new friends. When do more than 100 people have it?
steps: Monday: 5 new people. Total 5.
Tuesday: each of the 5 sends to 2: 10 new. Total 15.
Wednesday: 20 new. Total 35. Thursday: 40 new. Total 75.
Friday: 80 new. Total 155. That's over 100.
b2018-17.check: Thursday's total is 75 (not yet 100), Friday's is 155. ✓
b2018-17.spot: Things doubling? Make a table day by day.
b2018-17.oops: Only counting the new people each day instead of the total.

b2018-20.ask: Four ladybugs on a grid. One sleeps and never moves. The others move to a neighbouring cell each whistle, never straight back. What might the grid look like after the 4th whistle?
steps: Find the sleeping ladybug: compare the start with after the 1st whistle. Only one cell has a ladybug both times. That's the sleeper.
Each other ladybug steps up, down, left or right each whistle, and never straight back to the cell it just left.
Check the answers against the picture after the 3rd whistle: E moves the sleeper; D needs a two-cell jump; C needs a diagonal step; B sends a ladybug back to where it came from.
Only A follows every rule.
b2018-20.check: In A, the sleeper is in place and every other ladybug is one legal step away. ✓
b2018-20.spot: Step-by-step moves? Find what never changes first.
b2018-20.oops: Forgetting a ladybug can't go back to the cell it just left.

b2018-21.ask: From 3, 5, 2, 6, 1, 4, 7, Masha picks three numbers adding to 8, and Dasha picks three adding to 7. How many numbers do they share?
steps: Three different numbers adding to 7: only 1 + 2 + 4. So Dasha has 1, 2, 4.
Three different numbers adding to 8: 1 + 2 + 5, or 1 + 3 + 4.
Compare with Dasha: 1, 2, 5 shares 1 and 2. 1, 3, 4 shares 1 and 4.
Either way they share 2 numbers.
b2018-21.check: Both of Masha's options share exactly two numbers with 1, 2, 4. ✓
b2018-21.spot: Only a few options? List them all and check each.
b2018-21.oops: Thinking you can't tell because Masha has two options.

b2018-22.ask: Five balls weigh 30, 50, 50, 50 and 80 g. Use the scales to find the 30 g ball.
steps: Look at the third scale: two balls on one side balance three balls on the other.
All five balls add to 260 g. Balanced means each side is 130 g.
Two balls making 130: must be 80 + 50. Three balls making 130: 50 + 50 + 30.
Use the other scales to see which ball in the group of three is lighter: it's C.
b2018-22.check: With C = 30 g, every scale in the picture tips the right way. ✓
b2018-22.spot: Balance scales? Start with the one that balances.
b2018-22.oops: Ignoring which side is heavier on the tipped scales.

b2018-23.ask: A biggest-possible 6-digit number uses A three times, B twice and C once. Which pattern can it never be?
steps: To make the biggest number, put the biggest digits first.
Equal digits will always be next to each other: you'd put all the copies of the biggest digit first, then the next, and so on.
AAABCB splits the two Bs with a C in between.
If B were bigger than C, BB would come before C. If C were bigger, C would come before BB. So AAABCB never happens.
b2018-23.check: The other patterns keep equal digits together, so they can happen with the right digits. ✓
b2018-23.spot: Biggest number from digits? Biggest digits first, and equal digits stay together.
b2018-23.oops: Trying lots of actual numbers instead of thinking about the pattern.

b2018-24.ask: Kate + Mom = 36 years. Mom + Granny = 81 years. How old was Granny when Kate was born?
steps: Both sums have Mom. Take the first away from the second: (Mom + Granny) − (Kate + Mom) = Granny − Kate.
Granny is 45 years older than Kate, so she was 45 when Kate was born.
b2018-24.spot: Two sums sharing a person? Subtract them and the shared person disappears.
b2018-24.oops: Trying to find everyone's exact age.

b2018-25.ask: Split 2 to 10 into groups with equal sums. Most groups possible?
steps: The group with 10 has a sum of at least 10. So each group's sum is at least 10.
The sum must divide 54 evenly and be at least 10: 18, 27 or 54. The smallest is 18, which gives 54 ÷ 18 = 3 groups.
b2018-25.spot: Equal groups? The total must divide evenly, and the biggest piece sets a minimum.
b2018-25.oops: Choosing 6 groups of 9: the 10 can't fit in a group of 9.

b2018-27.ask: Fill a 5 × 5 table with 0s and 1s so every 2 × 2 square has exactly three equal numbers. Biggest total?
steps: Each 2 × 2 square has three equal numbers and one different. To make the total big, use three 1s and one 0.
So every 2 × 2 square needs at least one 0.
You can fit four 2 × 2 squares that don't overlap in a 5 × 5 table. Each needs its own 0: at least four 0s.
25 − 4 = 21, and you can arrange it so it works.
b2018-27.check: Put 0s in a spread-out pattern (e.g. the second and fourth cells of rows 2 and 4): every 2 × 2 square has exactly one 0. ✓
b2018-27.spot: Biggest total with a rule for small squares? Count how many small squares don't overlap.
b2018-27.oops: Thinking some 2 × 2 squares can be all 1s.

b2018-28.ask: 14 people around a table, each a liar or truth-teller. Each says 'Both my neighbours are liars.' Most liars possible?
steps: A truth-teller really has two liar neighbours.
A liar's sentence is false, so at least one neighbour is a truth-teller. Three liars in a row would make the middle one truthful, which can't happen.
So liars come in groups of at most 2, with a truth-teller between groups: T L L T L L ...
14 seats: 4 groups of T L L (12 seats, 8 liars) + T L (1 more liar) = 9 liars.
b2018-28.check: 10 liars would need groups bigger than 2 somewhere, which breaks the rule. ✓
b2018-28.spot: Liars around a table? Work out what pattern of neighbours each type needs.
b2018-28.oops: Saying 14 or 10 without checking the liars' sentences must be false.

b2018-30.ask: Put 3 to 9 in seven circles: three lines through the centre circle, each with equal sums. Add up all possible centre numbers.
steps: Adding all three lines counts the centre 3 times and every other number once: 42 + 2 × centre.
That must divide by 3 (three equal lines). 42 already divides by 3, so 2 × centre must too: centre = 3, 6 or 9.
All three work. 3 + 6 + 9 = 18.
b2018-30.spot: Lines meeting in the middle? Add all lines and see how often the centre is counted.
b2018-30.oops: Finding one centre and stopping. The question asks for all of them.
